The product

Meet Solvere. Turn it around.

A small set of devices for an older person's home or care-home room. They notice when something is wrong, ask if she's okay in the room she's in, and send a real person when she needs one. No cameras. Nothing to wear. Nothing to charge.

3D needs WebGL. Showing a photo of the kit instead.

Drag to turn · Scroll or pinch to zoom · Tap the dots

Power

Powered by what's already there.

A radar that must never miss a fall is on all the time. Seeed lists 0.5 to 1.4 W for its kit: 12 to 34 Wh a day. Batteries would run flat in days. So every device plugs into a socket the home already has, at the height it already is.

Setup

Four steps. No tools. About 15 minutes.

A son or daughter can do it on a visit, or guide it by video from another city.

    She's in charge

    Things she can say

      Consent

      She agrees in her own words.

      At setup the hub explains what it does and asks her. If dementia means she can't decide, her legal proxy (power of attorney or healthcare proxy) does, and it's recorded. She can change what's shared any time.

      The safety net

      From a fall to a person at the door.

      Fixed rules decide every step, not AI. Each step has a clock. If nobody answers, the next step starts on its own.

        What 911 receives

        Possible fall · no answerUrgent
        Where
        12 Maple Ct, Apt 4 · bathroom
        What
        Fall at 2:21 am, no movement, asked twice
        Her notes
        81 · type 2 diabetes · blood thinner
        Door
        One-time code 4 8 1 9 · valid 30 min
        Sample data. Sent through a 911 data partner (RapidSOS-type link).

        Getting in

        The door is locked. She's on the floor.

        A smart lock or key lockbox. A one-time code goes only to the person who accepted, lasts 30 minutes, and is logged. She agrees to this at setup.

        Talk to her

        "Mom, Asha is 4 minutes away."

        Family or the responder can speak through the device nearest to her, so she's never alone on the floor wondering if anyone knows.

        Care homes

        Built for the building, not bolted on.

        Assisted living, memory care and nursing homes. In a typical 100-bed nursing home, 100 to 200 falls are reported every year, and half to three-quarters of residents fall (CDC).

        Solvere Intelligence

        Our own AI. It gets better with every home.

        Not a borrowed voice assistant. One agent, built end to end for older adults, from the radar signal to the words she hears.

        What's real today

        • 3D designs for every device (hub, bath pod, bedside pod, ceiling pod, tags), built around real parts: Seeed MR60 radar (25 × 31.5 mm), Home Assistant Voice PE (84 × 84 × 21 mm), a standard US plug (NEMA 5-15).
        • Radar windows 1.47 mm thick with a 2.5 mm air gap, from Seeed's own radome formula.
        • Printable files for every part, checked in code for fit, holes and tilt.
        • Power placed where US code already puts it: the sink outlet (NEC 210.52(D)).
        • This app, console and simulator as clickable prototypes.

        What's still ahead

        • Partners to sign: monitoring center, 911 data link, glucose data access, nurse call and EHR.
        • Certification: FCC radar testing, UL/ETL safety listing.
        • Pilot proof: falls seen from the bath pod, pets, two-person homes.
        • Times like "help in 6 minutes" are examples, not promises yet.

        Who pays

        Four ways in.

        Families

        A monthly plan for a parent living on their own: the devices, the app, and a person who comes.

        Care homes

        Per bed. Every room looked after without cameras, and staff sent to the right door first.

        Medicaid waivers

        48 states and DC already pay for emergency response systems through home care waivers: typically $25 to $75 a month, plus setup.

        Health programs

        Medicare's ACCESS model pays $90 to $420 per patient per year for better chronic care. Our cuff and glucose trends fit it.
